generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, an essay is expected to argue, not just describe. A question such as whether a therapy works wants a reasoned position, built from the evidence and shaped by the relevant literature. The argument is carried by structure: the introduction states what you will argue, each body paragraph makes one point supported by studies, and the conclusion draws the case together. Writing well across genres, from essays to lab reports, is itself a mark of a strong psychology student.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students writing the introduction to an essay on the same question.

Tom opens with two broad sentences about why the topic matters, then lists what the essay will look at. It reads smoothly, but it never says what he will argue. His reader reaches the body with no sense of a position, so each study arrives as a separate point rather than a step in a case. This is structure without an argument.

Amara introduces the topic, notes briefly how the literature tends to treat it, and ends with a clear line of argument: what she will argue, and why. Now her body has something to carry. Each paragraph makes one point that advances the argument, and the reader can follow the case building. This is structure doing its job.

Both introductions are well written. Only Amara used the structure to set up an argument the rest of the essay could carry.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, the argumentative essay is a continuous response built around one argument, and that argument is carried by structure. The introduction states the line of argument, the body makes one point per paragraph, and the conclusion synthesises them. You can now recognise the argument in each part and say what a strong introduction must do. The next lesson shows how studies are woven in to support it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's introduction stronger than Tom's?

items.text: It ended with a clear line of argument, so the body had a case to carry.
It was longer and used more technical psychology terms.
It listed everything the essay would look at.
It avoided mentioning the psychological literature.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara stated a line of argument, so each paragraph could advance it.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what let Amara's body build a case rather than offer separate points.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's introduction ended with a clear line of argument. Tom's listed topics and stated no case.
